h1: Hydraulic Hose and Fittings
ozet: Hydraulic hose: 1SN, 2SN, 2SC, 4SP, 4SH and R6 types. Gates, Alfagomma, HansaFlex and Vereks. On-site crimping, same-day service.
giris:
Hydraulic hose is the flexible connecting element that carries fluid through the system without losing pressure. Selecting the right hose depends on three values: working pressure, fluid temperature, and inner diameter. Getting any one of these wrong leads to premature hose fatigue or a risk of rupture.

Hidroteknik stocks 1SN and 2SN single/double-wire-braided hose, 4SP and 4SH multi-spiral hose, and thermoplastic hose types at its warehouse in Denizli. Hose crimping is done in-house; standard sizes are generally delivered the same day.

The Forcestream, Seltex, and Ultimate lines, along with general-purpose hoses such as washing, spraying, and fuel applications, belong to the Sel code family and are listed in a separate group: see "Sel Hose".

sss.s: What is the difference between 1SN and 2SN hose?
sss.c: 1SN has a single steel wire braid and is intended for medium-pressure applications. 2SN has a double wire braid and withstands roughly twice the working pressure at the same inner diameter. At the same size, 2SN has a larger outer diameter and bend radius; this should be taken into account in tight installations.

sss.s: How is hydraulic hose size determined?
sss.c: Size is specified by the hose's inner diameter (for example DN12, 1/2 inch). Flow rate and inner diameter together determine flow velocity; pressure lines are generally kept in the 3-6 m/s range. If the inner diameter is chosen too small, pressure loss and heating increase.

sss.s: Is hose crimping done the same day?
sss.c: For standard size and fitting combinations, crimping is generally completed the same day. Turnaround varies for jobs requiring custom lengths, special fittings, or out-of-stock types; contact our sales team for exact timing.

sss.s: What is the service life of a hydraulic hose?
sss.c: Hose service life depends on working pressure, temperature, bend radius, and vibration. Periodic inspection is recommended for lines that run continuously at maximum pressure. Cracking, blistering, or exposed wire on the outer cover indicates the hose needs to be replaced.

h1: Industrial and Special-Purpose Hose
ozet: Water, hot water, suction, fuel, spraying and washdown hose; transparent spiral-reinforced suction lines.
giris:
This group covers the hoses outside the hydraulic circuit. A hydraulic hose is chosen by pressure; here what matters is the fluid carried and the temperature. Fuel hose needs an inner tube that resists the fuel, hot-water hose a temperature limit, spraying hose chemical resistance.

Transparent spiral-reinforced hose is used on suction lines: the rigid helix stops the hose collapsing on itself under vacuum. Being transparent lets you see what is passing through, which is why it is preferred in food, agriculture and waste transfer.

If you are looking for hydraulic hose, that is a separate group — working pressure, braid layers and coupling type are listed there.

sss.s: What is the difference between Forcestream, Seltex, and Ultimate?
sss.c: All three are single/double-braided medium-pressure hydraulic hose lines and can be used interchangeably within the same pressure classes (R1AT/1SN, R2AT/2SN). The difference between them is the manufacturer line — the technical class is the same; whichever is in stock is shipped, and substitution causes no issue as long as size and pressure class match.

sss.s: Why are Sel hoses on a separate page?
sss.c: Sel is a code family that groups both hydraulic pressure lines and general-purpose hoses — such as washing, spraying, and fuel — under the same code. Since this mixed structure would disrupt the scope of the hydraulic hose and pneumatic hose pages, it is listed on its own page.

sss.s: What sizing information is needed for non-pressure hoses (water, spraying, washing)?
sss.c: Inner diameter (usually in inches: 3/8, 1/2, 3/4) and length are sufficient. For lines carrying chemicals (spraying, fuel), specify the substance being carried; the inner lining material varies accordingly.

sss.s: What are spiral wrap guards and hose end fittings?
sss.c: A spiral wrap guard is a polyethylene wrap that covers the hose on the outside to protect it against abrasion and scuffing; it is not the hose itself. The hose end fitting is the hard plastic/metal coupling body fitted onto the hose end. Both are sold as separate stock items and can also be ordered together with the hose.

h1: Hydraulic Fittings and Connectors
ozet: Hydraulic fittings in metric, BSP/BSPT and ORFS thread types. Over 1,400 items including elbows, nipples, plugs and swivel fittings.
giris:
A fitting is the component that joins the parts of a hydraulic line together in a leak-tight manner. The most common mistake in the industry stems from how similar different thread standards look: metric, BSP, BSPT, ORFS, and JIC threads can look nearly identical to the eye, but their sealing principles differ.

BSP is a parallel thread whose seal is typically made with a gasket or a cone seat, while BSPT is a tapered thread where the thread itself forms the seal. ORFS, on the other hand, uses face sealing via an O-ring and is preferred in high-vibration systems. A mismatched thread will leak under initial pressure or damage the threads.

sss.s: What is the difference between BSP and BSPT?
sss.c: BSP is a parallel (straight) thread; sealing is provided not by the thread itself but by a gasket, O-ring, or cone-seat face. BSPT, on the other hand, is tapered; as the thread is tightened, a wedging effect creates the seal. Since they share the same pitch, the two can be screwed together, but this combination does not provide a reliable seal.

sss.s: Where are ORFS fittings used?
sss.c: ORFS (O-Ring Face Seal) provides sealing with an O-ring compressed between two flat faces. It is preferred in construction equipment and mobile hydraulic applications with high vibration, because it is more reliable than thread sealing.

sss.s: How do I determine fitting size?
sss.c: Thread outer diameter is measured with calipers, and thread pitch is determined with a thread gauge. Measuring diameter alone is not enough — threads of the same diameter can have different pitches. When in doubt, the fastest way is to bring in the existing part and show it to our sales team.

h1: ORFS Fittings (O-Ring Face Seal)
ozet: ORFS straight, elbow, tee, and plug fittings. 230+ items for high-vibration mobile hydraulic applications.
giris:
ORFS (O-Ring Face Seal) is a connection system that achieves sealing not through the thread but with an O-ring compressed between two flat faces. This detail becomes decisive in high-vibration applications: connections relying on thread sealing tend to loosen over time under vibration, whereas in ORFS the sealing element is independent of the thread.

For this reason, ORFS is the common standard in construction equipment, agricultural machinery, and mobile hydraulics. During assembly, care should be taken that the O-ring seats properly in its groove and that the faces are free of burrs; if the O-ring is pinched or pushed out of its groove, the connection will leak under initial pressure. Keeping spare O-rings on hand saves time in the field.

sss.s: Why is ORFS considered more reliable than JIC?
sss.c: JIC 37° seals via conical surface contact; vibration and repeated assembly fatigue this surface over time. In ORFS, sealing is achieved with an elastomer O-ring, making it more tolerant of surface variation and vibration. This is why it is preferred in mobile hydraulics.

sss.s: What material should the ORFS O-ring be made of?
sss.c: NBR is sufficient for standard mineral-based hydraulic oil. FKM (Viton) is chosen for high temperatures or special fluids. When replacing an O-ring, the material must be correct in addition to the size.

sss.s: My ORFS connection is leaking — what should I check first?
sss.c: Almost always the O-ring. It may have popped out of its groove, been pinched, cut, or gone missing. Tightening the nut further is not the solution — over-tightening cuts the O-ring. The connection should be disassembled and the O-ring visually inspected.

h1: Nipples, Connectors, and Adapters
ozet: Coupling nipples, reducing nipples, extension nipples, and transition adapters; 570+ items in BSP, metric, and UNF threads.
giris:
A nipple is a male-male threaded part that joins two threaded connections together. In hydraulic and pneumatic lines it is often the unsung hero: it lets two pieces of equipment made to different standards be connected to each other without disrupting the line.

A coupling nipple is the simplest type, with both ends the same size. On a reducing nipple, the ends are different sizes, and it serves to change diameter. Extension nipples move a connection to an accessible point in tight installations. When selecting a nipple, not only the thread size but also the thread standard must match — BSP and metric threads of the same diameter can be screwed together, but they will not seal.

sss.s: Does a reducing nipple weaken the line?
sss.c: No, not when correctly selected. However, reducing the diameter increases flow velocity; if several reductions are used in succession along a long line, pressure loss and heating become noticeable. Where possible, the diameter change should be made at a single point.

sss.s: Should I wrap the nipple with PTFE tape to prevent leaking?
sss.c: On tapered threads (BSPT, NPT), a thin layer of PTFE tape or liquid sealant is appropriate. On parallel threads (BSP), sealing is provided by a gasket or O-ring; wrapping tape there is not a solution and strains the thread. The thread type must be identified first.

sss.s: Can an extension nipple withstand pressure?
sss.c: Yes, as long as it stays within the catalog pressure rating. The point to watch is the leverage effect created by its length: in vibrating applications, a long nipple puts extra load on the connection point and should be supported where possible.

h1: Hydraulic Blanking Plugs and Plugs
ozet: BSP, metric, UNF and ORFS blanking plugs; hex socket and hex head types, 220+ items.
giris:
A blanking plug is a simple but safety-critical component that seals off an unused port. An empty manifold outlet, a port left open after testing, or a spare connection point must always be closed with a pressure-rated plug — improvised fixes can blow out under pressure and create a hazard.

Thread standard and sealing method follow the same logic as fittings when selecting a plug: on tapered threads such as BSPT, the thread itself provides the seal, while parallel threads such as BSP require a gasket or O-ring. Hex socket (internal hex) types don't protrude above the surface, making them suited to tight assemblies, while hex head (external hex) types allow higher torque with a wrench, making them preferred for larger diameters.

sss.s: Is there a difference between a blanking plug and a regular plug?
sss.c: A blanking plug is fully closed and permanently seals the port. Vented or breather plugs, by contrast, are used on tanks and housings for pressure equalization. Mixing the two up means either the system can't breathe, or a port that should stay sealed is left open.

sss.s: Should I choose hex socket or hex head?
sss.c: Hex socket heads suit tight spaces and assemblies where nothing should protrude above the surface. For larger diameters and applications requiring higher tightening torque, hex head types are safer, since a wrench gives easier access.

sss.s: What pressure rating does a plug withstand?
sss.c: A plug's rated pressure matches the class of the fitting family it belongs to. The plug must therefore be selected to match the pressure class of the line — a lower-rated plug on a high-pressure manifold creates a safety weak point.

h1: Hydraulic Valves: Directional Control, Pressure, Check and Flow Control Valves
ozet: Directional control, pressure control, check and flow control valves. NG6/NG10 modular valves, in-line load-holding and lock valves. Pneumatic valves are a separate category.
giris:
A valve is the component that determines where, how much, and at what pressure fluid flows in a hydraulic or pneumatic circuit. It's the "decision-maker" of the circuit: the cylinder produces force, the pump supplies flow, but the valve determines the direction and speed of motion.

There are three main families. Directional control valves select which line the flow goes to (referred to by port/position designations such as 4/2, 4/3). Pressure valves handle safety and regulation; the relief valve limits the system's maximum pressure. Flow control valves determine speed. Modular NG6 and NG10 valves allow these to be stacked together to build a compact circuit.

sss.s: Are a relief valve and a pressure-reducing valve the same thing?
sss.c: No. The relief valve protects the entire system; once the set pressure is exceeded, it diverts excess flow to the tank. A pressure-reducing valve, on the other hand, holds the pressure in one branch at a lower value independent of the rest of the system. One is for protection, the other for regulation.

sss.s: What do 4/2 and 4/3 valve mean?
sss.c: The first number gives the number of ports, the second the number of positions. A 4/3 valve has four ports and three positions; its center position allows the cylinder to be stopped under load. A 4/2 valve has no center position — the cylinder is always commanded in one direction or the other.

sss.s: Should I look at flow rate when selecting a pneumatic valve?
sss.c: Yes. In pneumatics, a valve's flow capacity is given by its Cv or Kv value. If a valve with insufficient flow capacity is chosen relative to the cylinder volume and desired cycle time, the cylinder will run slowly; choosing a valve larger than the line size is also an unnecessary cost.

h1: Solenoid Valve Coils: 12/24 V DC and 110/220 V AC Replacement Coils
ozet: Replacement coils for hydraulic and pneumatic solenoid valves: 12 and 24 V DC, 110 and 220 V AC; bore sizes from Ø9 to 31.6 mm, NG06 and NG10 valve coils.
giris:
A solenoid valve consists of two parts: the body that directs the oil or air, and the electromagnet — the coil — that moves the spool inside it. The coil is the part of the valve that talks to the electrical system, and it is the part that fails most often. That is why it is sold separately: the body may be sound while the coil has burnt out, or a machine may have been moved to a different supply voltage so that only the coil needs changing.

Ordering a replacement coil calls for three pieces of information. First, voltage and current type: 12 V DC and 24 V DC on mobile machinery and PLC-controlled circuits, 110 V AC and 220 V AC in fixed industrial plant. Fitting a coil of the wrong voltage burns it out in seconds; putting 220 V on a 24 V coil is the most common and most expensive of these mistakes.

Second, the diameter and height of the bore that sits over the valve pin. Stock covers Ø9, Ø10, 13, 14.85, 16, 21.1, 23.2, 26.2 and 31.6 mm. This dimension is printed in the product name in millimetres and governs fit regardless of brand — coils of the same size from different makers will usually interchange. On modular hydraulic valves the size is quoted by valve size directly: NG06 (Cetop 3) valves take 23.2 mm class coils, NG10 (Cetop 5) valves take the 31.6 mm class.

Third, power and protection rating. AC coils are rated in VA, DC coils in W (18 VA, 28 W and so on). Coils rated IP65 withstand dust and water jets; that rating should be insisted on outdoors and on machines that are washed down. Connector type should also be stated when ordering; some coils come with an LED connector fitted.

The two most common causes of a burnt coil are a spool jammed by dirt in the body, and a supply voltage that runs persistently high. When the spool sticks, the coil converts the load it cannot move into heat and the winding cooks. For that reason, when coils burn one after another the culprit is usually not the coil but a valve body that needs cleaning.

sss.s: How do I determine coil size?
sss.c: What matters is the diameter of the bore that fits over the valve pin, and the coil height; both appear in the product name in millimetres (14.85 mm or 23.2 mm, for instance). Remove the old coil and take those two measurements with calipers, and a compatible coil can be found regardless of brand.

sss.s: What do NG06 and NG10 mean?
sss.c: NG06 and NG10 are mounting-interface standards for modular hydraulic valves (also known as Cetop 3 and Cetop 5). The coils for these valve sizes are standardised in turn: 23.2 mm class for NG06, 31.6 mm class for NG10. The information is printed on the valve label.

sss.s: My coils keep burning out — why?
sss.c: When coils fail one after another the problem is usually in the valve body, not the coil. A spool jammed by dirt or by particles in the oil cannot move under the coil's magnetic field; the coil turns the load it cannot shift into heat and the winding cooks. Fitting a new coil without cleaning the body gives the same result. The second cause is a supply voltage persistently above the coil rating.

sss.s: Can a 220 V coil replace a 24 V coil?
sss.c: No. Voltage and current type (DC/AC) must match the coil label exactly. A coil of the wrong voltage either will not pull in at all or burns out within seconds. Because the same body is produced with coils in several voltages, a coil fitting physically does not mean it fits electrically.

sss.s: Why does the IP65 rating matter?
sss.c: IP65 means the coil is dust-tight and withstands water jets from any direction. That rating should be required on machines working outdoors and in food and textile plants that are washed down with pressurised water. Inside a dry enclosure, a lower rating is adequate.

h1: Hydraulic Pumps and Power Units
ozet: Gear and axial piston hydraulic pumps; tandem sets and power unit components.
giris:
A hydraulic pump doesn't produce pressure — it produces flow. Pressure arises from the resistance this flow encounters. This distinction matters in practice: when pressure is low in a system, the problem is often not the pump but a leak or the relief valve setting.

The most common type is the gear pump: simple, inexpensive, and tolerant of contamination, with fixed displacement. Axial piston pumps reach higher pressures and, being capable of variable displacement, can produce only as much flow as needed, saving energy. Selection requires weighing speed (rpm), displacement (cc/rev) and working pressure together; an undersized suction line is the most common cause of shortened pump life.

sss.s: How is pump flow rate calculated?
sss.c: Flow rate (L/min) ≈ displacement (cc/rev) × speed (rpm) ÷ 1000, multiplied by volumetric efficiency. For example, a pump with 20 cc/rev displacement delivers approximately 29 L/min at 1450 rpm. The actual value drops somewhat depending on efficiency and pressure.

sss.s: The pump is running noisily — what could be the cause?
sss.c: The most common cause is cavitation: a narrow suction line, a clogged filter, low oil level, or oil that is too cold and overly viscous. An air leak on the suction side produces the same sound. The suction side should always be checked before the pressure side.

sss.s: Gear pump or piston pump?
sss.c: If fixed flow is sufficient and pressure is moderate, a gear pump is both economical and durable. If high pressure, variable flow, or energy efficiency matters, an axial piston pump is preferred; the initial investment is higher.

sss.s: Do you stock PZB pumps?
sss.c: Yes. The PZB straight-piston (P1) and bent-axis (EOS) pump lines are held in stock. Send us the code on your pump’s label and we will match it.

h1: Hydraulic Motors (Orbital): Low-Speed High-Torque Motors
ozet: Orbital hydraulic motors; low-speed high-torque motors for mixers, conveyors, cranes, agricultural and cleaning machinery.
giris:
A hydraulic motor does the opposite of a hydraulic pump: where the pump turns mechanical rotation into pressure, the motor turns pressure into mechanical rotation. A cylinder gives linear motion; a hydraulic motor gives continuous rotation — conveyor drums, mixer impellers, crane winches, sweeper brushes and agricultural drive shafts all turn on hydraulic motors.

Most of the motors in stock are of the orbital (gerotor) type. In this design an inner gear tracks eccentrically inside an outer gear ring; because a large number of chambers fill and empty on each revolution, shaft speed is low and torque is high. That characteristic — direct drive — removes the need for a gearbox in most applications and saves considerable space.

Displacement sits at the centre of the selection: the volume of oil the motor swallows per revolution, in cm³/rev. The number in the product code is exactly that figure (HMR.100 = 100 cm³/rev). Speed follows from it: speed (rpm) ≈ flow (l/min) × 1000 ÷ displacement (cm³). So 40 l/min turns a 100 cm³/rev motor at roughly 400 rpm. If slower, stronger rotation is wanted at the same flow, choose a larger displacement; if speed is wanted, choose a smaller one.

The second determinant is torque, which comes from working pressure: torque ≈ pressure (bar) × displacement (cm³) ÷ 63. The third is the shaft and mounting geometry — plain, splined and keyed shafts, and flange hole patterns, decide whether the motor bolts onto the machine; this has to be specified alongside displacement when ordering.

When building a hydraulic motor circuit, leaving the return line free to tank matters, because it lets the motor draw oil during the moments it keeps turning under its own inertia; otherwise the motor cavitates internally. For the pump that drives the motor see «Hydraulic Pumps», and for direction and speed control see «Hydraulic Valves».

sss.s: How is hydraulic motor speed calculated?
sss.c: Speed is flow divided by displacement: speed (rpm) ≈ flow (l/min) × 1000 ÷ displacement (cm³/rev). A pump delivering 40 l/min, for example, turns a 100 cm³/rev motor at roughly 400 rpm. Actual speed falls slightly below this figure because of internal leakage.

sss.s: What does the number in the code mean?
sss.c: The number in codes such as HMR.100 or MR200 is the motor's displacement, the volume of oil it swallows per revolution (cm³/rev). This single figure sets both speed and torque: at the same flow, a large displacement turns more slowly but more powerfully, a small displacement faster but weaker.

sss.s: Hydraulic motor or geared electric motor?
sss.c: Where hydraulic power is already available and space is tight, the hydraulic motor has the advantage: it delivers high torque directly, needs no gearbox, is protected from mechanical damage by the relief valve when overloaded, and its speed is infinitely variable. In fixed installations running at constant speed, an electric motor is more efficient.

sss.s: Will a hydraulic motor run in both directions?
sss.c: Most orbital motors run both ways; a directional valve that swaps the inlet and outlet lines reverses rotation. On models with a drain line, however, that line must be connected freely to tank under all conditions. On special models built for one direction only, the direction marked on the label must be observed.

sss.s: The motor has lost speed and power — what could it be?
sss.c: The most common cause is increased internal leakage: a worn gerotor set lets oil past from the pressure side to the return side, and torque and speed fall together. The second cause is reduced pump flow — in that case the other functions in the system slow down too. To tell them apart, measure pressure and flow in the line feeding the motor.

h1: Hydraulic Oil Filters: Suction and Return Filters with Elements
ozet: Suction filters from 25 to 750 l/min, tank-top and in-line return filters, complete filter assemblies and replacement filter elements.
giris:
The great majority of hydraulic faults come down to a single cause: dirt in the oil. Metal particles shed by wear, dust introduced during assembly and rubber crumbs from seals circulate through the micron-scale clearances of pump and valves. The filter is the only element that breaks this cycle, and although it is one of the cheapest parts in the system, neglecting it produces the most expensive damage.

A filter occupies one of three positions in the circuit. The suction filter works at the pump inlet, submerged in the tank; it is a coarse filter and protects the pump from large particles. Its rating is given in l/min (25, 45, 65, 90, 125, 180, 225, 300, 500, 750) and must not be selected below the pump flow. Its dimensions are listed as length, diameter and thread (L:160 D:61 A:1, for instance), because it has to fit inside the tank.

The return filter comes into play as oil flows back to the tank. It is a fine filter, and since all the circulating oil passes through it, it does the real cleaning. Tank-top versions simplify mounting. The pressure line filter is used after the pump, immediately ahead of a sensitive valve that needs protecting; it gives the finest filtration, but its housing is built to withstand full system pressure.

The second axis of selection is pore size, given in microns and visible in the product code (C25 = 25 micron). A finer filter delivers cleaner oil but clogs sooner and causes more pressure drop. Typical values are 100–125 micron on suction and 10–25 micron on return.

Filters are sold either as complete housings or as elements alone. Routine maintenance normally changes the element while the housing stays in place. A clogged suction filter creates a vacuum at the pump inlet, bubbles form in the oil and the pump cavitates — this is the most common reason for a pump that runs with a growling noise. Read this page together with the fault notes on the «Hydraulic Pumps» page.

sss.s: Which matters more, the suction filter or the return filter?
sss.c: They do different jobs. The suction filter protects the pump from large particles and is coarse by necessity — it cannot be fine, because a pressure drop at the pump inlet causes cavitation. The real cleaning is done by the return filter: all the oil circulating in the system passes through it on its way back to tank. A healthy circuit has both.

sss.s: How is filter flow rating selected?
sss.c: The filter rating must not be below the pump flow. On the suction side this rule is especially strict: an undersized filter creates a vacuum at the pump inlet and leads to cavitation. On the return side, allow for the surge of flow produced as a cylinder retracts and choose one size up.

sss.s: What does the micron value mean?
sss.c: It is the size of the smallest particle the filter will stop; it appears in the code as C25, meaning 25 micron. A smaller number means finer filtration. Typical values are 100–125 micron on suction and 10–25 micron on return. A filter finer than needed clogs quickly and opens its bypass valve, leaving the system running unfiltered.

sss.s: How often should a filter be changed?
sss.c: Go by the contamination indicator rather than by elapsed time. Where an indicator is fitted, change the element when the needle enters the red zone. Without one, make the first change within the first 50 hours after commissioning — that element collects the assembly debris — and thereafter typically every 500 to 1000 hours. The filter must always be changed with the oil.

sss.s: Should I buy a complete filter or just the element?
sss.c: If the housing is sound the element alone is enough, and that is what routine maintenance changes. A complete filter is bought for a new installation, for a cracked housing, or when moving to a different flow. When ordering an element, state both the housing type and the micron value — elements of the same size are produced in several pore ratings.

sss.s: The pump growls — could the filter be involved?
sss.c: Very likely. A clogged suction filter creates a vacuum at the pump inlet; vapour bubbles form in the oil and collapse in the pressure zone. This phenomenon, cavitation, produces the characteristic growl and eats the pump from the inside. The first places to check are the suction filter and the oil level.

h1: Hydraulic Oil Coolers: 60–220 l/min Fan-Cooled Oil-to-Air Heat Exchangers
ozet: Fan-cooled hydraulic oil coolers in 12 V, 24 V and 220 V; flow capacity from 60 to 220 l/min, body sizes from 240×240×45 to 720×700×63 mm.
giris:
Part of the energy spent in a hydraulic system never comes out as work; it turns into heat. Some power is lost as heat at every throttling valve, in the oil returning through the relief valve, in the pump's internal leakage and in every friction along the line. On small systems the surface of the tank and the pipework is enough to shed that heat; as the system grows or the duty cycle tightens it is not, and the oil starts to warm.

Thinning oil brings trouble in a chain. As viscosity falls, internal leakage in pump and valves rises, the system slows and generates still more heat — a loop that feeds itself. The oil film thins, metal surfaces come closer together and wear accelerates. Seals harden at high temperature, lose elasticity and begin to leak. The oil itself oxidises; it darkens, turns acidic and leaves a varnish deposit. The practical threshold is around 60 °C: a system that runs continuously above that is asking for a cooler.

The coolers in stock are of the oil-to-air type: the oil passes through a matrix while a fan blows air across it to carry the heat away. Selection turns on three values. First, the flow to be cooled (80–220 l/min); the cooler's capacity is set by the flow passing through the line. Second, the fan voltage — 12 V and 24 V models run from the vehicle's own supply on mobile hydraulics, 220 V models from the mains in fixed installations. Third, the body size (from 240×240×45 to 720×700×63 mm); the space allotted to the cooler on the machine and the opening the fan draws air through are planned around it.

A cooler is normally connected in the return line, just before the oil enters the tank. Because the matrix is not designed to withstand full system pressure it should not be connected directly into a pressure line; it is also sensible to use a bypass check valve to protect the matrix during cold starts. Capacity drops quickly once the air-side face becomes dusty — periodic cleaning is the cheapest way to recover it.

sss.s: Does my hydraulic system need a cooler?
sss.c: It does if the oil temperature stays continuously above 60 °C. Measure at the tank, after the system has run at full load for a while. A system that settles around 50 °C does not need one. Even where temperature is acceptable, a cooler noticeably extends oil and seal life on short-cycle, high-duty machines.

sss.s: How is cooler capacity selected?
sss.c: Capacity is chosen from the flow that will pass through the cooler; items give it in l/min (80, 100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 220). For a return-line installation, allow for the peak instantaneous flow generated as a cylinder retracts. If capacity is too low the oil will not cool; there is no harm in oversizing beyond space and cost.

sss.s: What is the difference between 12 V, 24 V and 220 V?
sss.c: Only the fan motor supply differs; the cooling matrix is the same. The 12 V and 24 V models are fed from the vehicle's own electrical system on mobile hydraulics — tractors, construction machinery, truck-mounted equipment. The 220 V models connect to the mains in fixed industrial plant. Choosing the wrong voltage is the most common reason for a return.

sss.s: Where is the cooler connected?
sss.c: The standard position is the return line, with the oil passing through the cooler just before it enters the tank. Because the matrix housing is not designed for full system pressure it must not be connected directly into a pressure line. Fitting a parallel bypass check valve is sensible so that thick, cold oil does not strain the matrix on start-up.

sss.s: There is a cooler fitted but the oil still overheats — why?
sss.c: Look first at the air side of the matrix: once a mixture of dust and oil coats the surface, capacity drops quickly, and cleaning resolves most cases. There is also no cooling if the fan is not turning or is blowing the wrong way. If those are sound, there is simply too much heat being generated — usually oil returning continuously over the relief valve, or an oversized pump.

h1: Electric Motors for Hydraulic Power Units: 0.37–22 kW, 1500 rpm, B35 Flange
ozet: Three-phase and single-phase electric motors driving hydraulic power units: 0.37 kW to 22 kW, 1500 rpm (4-pole), 220 V and 380 V, foot-and-flange B35 frame.
giris:
In a fixed hydraulic power unit the electric motor is the first link in the chain: it converts mains electricity into rotation, that rotation drives the pump, and the pump pressurises the oil. Selecting the motor correctly determines whether the unit works at all and how long it lasts.

The first value in the selection is power, calculated from what the pump will demand: power (kW) ≈ pressure (bar) × flow (l/min) ÷ 600 (with an allowance for overall efficiency). A system asking for 20 l/min at 100 bar needs roughly 3.3 kW; a 4 kW motor is chosen as the next step up. An undersized motor labours under load, draws current and trips the overload; oversizing does no harm but reduces efficiency at part load and adds cost.

The second value is speed. Hydraulic power units almost always use a 1500 rpm — that is, 4-pole — motor. Because pump flow is directly proportional to speed (flow ≈ displacement × speed), the motor speed must match the rated flow of the pump selected. A 3000 rpm motor draws twice the flow from the same pump, but the pump's suction capability and its service life may not suit that.

The third value is voltage and phase count. 380 V three-phase motors are the industry standard and are preferred in practice at every power above 1.5 kW. 220 V single-phase models are used in workshops and small units where no three-phase supply is available; at the same power they have a larger frame, cost more and have lower starting torque.

The fourth value is the mounting type, which governs installation. B35 means a frame with both feet and a flange: the motor sits on the chassis by its feet and bolts to the pump adaptor by its front flange. This is the standard choice for hydraulic power units, because the pump couples directly to the motor shaft and alignment has to be maintained. For pump and adaptor selection see the «Hydraulic Pumps» page.

sss.s: How many kW do I need?
sss.c: Motor power is calculated from what the pump will demand: power (kW) ≈ pressure (bar) × flow (l/min) ÷ 600. That formula includes an approximate allowance for efficiency. A system asking for 20 l/min at 100 bar needs roughly 3.3 kW, so the next standard size, 4 kW, is chosen. On systems running continuously at full load, going one size up is the safe option.

sss.s: Why is 1500 rpm always used?
sss.c: Pump flow is directly proportional to speed, and the rated flows of hydraulic pumps are generally quoted at 1500 rpm. A 4-pole (1500 rpm) motor also runs more quietly than a 2-pole one and does not strain the pump's suction capability. High speed increases the risk of cavitation at the pump inlet.

sss.s: What does B35 mean?
sss.c: B35 is the mounting designation for a motor that has both a footed and a flanged frame. The motor sits on the chassis by its feet and bolts to the pump adaptor by its front flange. It is the standard choice for hydraulic power units: because the pump couples to the motor shaft, misalignment has to be prevented by the flange.

sss.s: 220 V single-phase or 380 V three-phase?
sss.c: If three-phase is available on site, 380 V is preferred: at the same power it gives a smaller frame, higher starting torque and better efficiency. 220 V single-phase models are used only where there is no three-phase supply, and generally remain reasonable up to about 3 kW.

sss.s: The motor overload keeps tripping — what could cause it?
sss.c: The most common cause is the system holding the motor at full load continuously: the pressure setting may be higher than needed, or the pump flow may be oversized for the motor. The second is cooling — if the rear fan cowl is blocked the windings overheat. The third is electrical: phase loss, low voltage, or an incorrectly set overload relay. Oil thickening in cold weather also raises the current on first start.

h1: Hydraulic Cylinder Manufacturing, Overhaul and Spare Parts
ozet: Custom hydraulic cylinder manufacturing and overhaul, built to your dimensions. Rear covers, steel caps, pistons, gland bushings and wear rings are machined in-house.
giris:
A hydraulic cylinder is the component that converts the energy of pressurized fluid into linear motion and force. The force it produces follows a simple relationship: force equals pressure times piston area. In the push direction the full piston area is active; in the pull direction the rod cross-section reduces the effective area, so the force obtained at the same pressure is smaller. When replacing a cylinder, it's necessary to look not only at the bore diameter but also at the rod diameter and mounting type.

We don't sell this product off the shelf — we manufacture it to your dimensions. Parts such as rear covers, cast and steel caps, threaded and bearing-mounted pistons, gland bushings and wear rings are machined in our own shop; this means we can also produce the equivalent of a non-standard length, a special mounting, or a cylinder that is no longer available.

For an overhaul, the cylinder is first disassembled and measured: rod wear, tube bore diameter and seal grooves are checked. Most failures don't require replacing the entire cylinder — they're resolved with a seal kit, a gland bushing, or a rod replacement. Bring in the cylinder you have; you don't need to know its dimensions.

sss.s: Do you have ready-made hydraulic cylinders in stock?
sss.c: We don't sell hydraulic cylinders from stock — we manufacture them to your dimensions. What we keep in stock are the parts used in manufacturing and overhaul: rear covers, steel and cast caps, pistons, gland bushings, wear rings. You give us the dimensions for the finished cylinder, and we produce it.

sss.s: How long does hydraulic cylinder manufacturing take?
sss.c: For standard bore diameters and mounting types, lead time is short since the parts are in stock; for jobs requiring custom dimensions, extra-long length, or a different mounting type, the timeframe varies. An exact lead time is given once measurements are taken.

sss.s: Should I have my cylinder repaired or have a new one made?
sss.c: If the tube bore and rod are sound, an overhaul is usually more economical: the seal kit, gland bushing, and if necessary the rod are renewed. If the tube has gone oval or the rod is deeply scored, new manufacturing is the better option. We'll tell you which makes sense once we've disassembled and measured it.

sss.s: How is cylinder force calculated?
sss.c: Push force = pressure × piston area. For example, a 63 mm diameter piston at 160 bar produces approximately 5 tons of push force. In the pull direction, force decreases because the rod cross-section reduces the effective area; with a 36 mm rod on the same cylinder, it drops to approximately 3.4 tons. You can use calculate.hidroteknik.com.tr to run the calculation.

h1: Chrome-Plated Rod, Induction-Hardened Rod, Honed Tube and Hydraulic Line Tube
ozet: Raw material for hydraulic cylinder manufacturing: Ø10–Ø220 chrome-plated and Ø8–Ø155 induction-hardened rod, honed tube from Ø40 to Ø350, hydraulic tubing from 5×1 to 42×4.
giris:
A hydraulic cylinder has three main parts: the barrel the piston travels inside, the rod that extends outward, and the seal set that keeps them tight. This page covers the raw material for the first two — the stock a workshop needs when it builds its own cylinders or refurbishes a worn one.

Chrome-plated rod is drawn steel bar with a hard chrome layer on the surface. The plating does two jobs: it reduces friction and wear, and it prevents corrosion. The wiper seal relies on the smoothness of that plating as it cleans dirt off the rod; once the plating is scored, the seal starts leaking within a short time. For this reason the rod must be protected from impact during handling and assembly. Induction-hardened rod has the steel beneath the plating hardened by induction; it stands up better to impact and side loading, which is why it is preferred in construction machinery and heavy-duty cylinders.

Honed tube forms the cylinder barrel. Its bore is ground on a honing machine to a cross-hatched finish; this texture lets the piston slide smoothly and gives the oil film a surface to hold on to. The size is always given as inner diameter × outer diameter (80 × 95, for instance): the bore determines the force the cylinder produces, the wall thickness determines the pressure it can withstand. Plain drawn tube cannot substitute for honed tube — the roughness of the bore will cut the seal on the very first stroke.

Hydraulic line tube is used for the fixed runs from pump to valve and from valve to cylinder; unlike hose it does not whip with vibration and lasts considerably longer. Its size is given as outer diameter × wall thickness (16 × 2, for instance), and the fitting is selected directly from that outer diameter: a 16 × 2 tube takes a 16L or 16S compression fitting. The tube and the fitting series (L light, S heavy) must match — otherwise the cutting ring does not grip the tube correctly.

Rod and tube items are listed together with their weight per metre (15.40 kg/m for 50 mm chrome-plated rod, for example); shipping and costing are worked out from that figure. For cut-to-length and machining see the «Hydraulic Cylinder» page, and for line connections see «Hydraulic Fittings».

sss.s: What is the difference between chrome-plated rod and induction-hardened rod?
sss.c: Both have a hard chrome surface; the difference is in the steel underneath. In chrome-plated rod the steel is left in its drawn condition. In induction-hardened rod the near-surface zone is heated by induction current and quenched, creating a hardened case that stops the plating from collapsing under impact and side load. Induction-hardened rod is used in construction machinery, tipper and heavy-duty cylinders; chrome-plated rod is used in ordinary industrial cylinders.

sss.s: How do I read a honed tube size?
sss.c: 80 × 95 means an 80 mm bore and a 95 mm outside diameter; the wall thickness is half the difference, that is 7.5 mm. Cylinder force is calculated from the bore (force = pressure × piston area), while pressure rating comes from the wall thickness. Giving only the bore when ordering is not enough — the same bore exists in several wall thicknesses.

sss.s: Which fitting size fits a hydraulic line tube?
sss.c: Compression fittings are selected by the tube's outer diameter. A 16 × 2 line tube needs a 16L (light series) or 16S (heavy series) fitting; the choice depends on working pressure. The L series suits roughly up to 160 bar, the S series higher pressures. Wall thickness must also suit the series: a heavy-series fitting can crush a thin-walled tube as it is tightened.

sss.s: What length does the rod come in?
sss.c: Rod and tube are stocked as bar and cut to the length you need. The kg/m figure shown next to each item is the weight per metre and is used for both pricing and shipping. A 50 mm chrome-plated rod is 15.40 kg/m, so a 2-metre piece weighs roughly 31 kg.

sss.s: Can a scored rod still be used?
sss.c: Not if the score runs lengthwise (along the axis) and is deep: the seal lip will continuously leak oil through that channel, and no amount of seal replacement will restore sealing. Shallow marks that cannot be felt with a fingernail cause no trouble. Where the chrome layer is flaking, the loose fragments will cut the seal; the rod must be replaced.

h1: Rod Ends: Threaded Clevis (PR) and Weld-On (S) Cylinder Mountings
ozet: Mounting components for hydraulic and pneumatic cylinders: PR20–PR110 threaded clevis rod ends, S series round (C) and rectangular (N) weld-on types.
giris:
A hydraulic cylinder is never bolted rigidly to its load. As the cylinder works, the axis of the load shifts, the machine frame flexes, and the line between the rod end and the rear mounting is thrown out. In a rigid connection that misalignment goes straight into the rod as a side load — and the rod is then carrying a force the seal and the bearing were never meant to take.

The consequence is well known in the field: the seal begins to leak on one side, the rod bends slightly over time, the plating scores. The replacement seal leaks again a few months later, because the seal was never the cause. A rod end is used precisely to release that misalignment — to let the cylinder swing with the load.

There are two types. The threaded clevis type (PR series) screws onto the thread at the end of the rod; the load pin passes through the jaw. The weld-on type (S series) is welded to the machine frame and comes in two sub-types: C with a round body, N with a rectangular one. The choice depends on the shape of the surface being welded to and how tight the space is.

The size figure is the diameter of the pin bore: 20 mm on a PR20, 50 mm on an S 50 N. It is selected from the pin that carries the load, not from the cylinder's rod diameter — confusing the two is a frequent mistake. On the threaded type the thread size at the rod end must match as well.

Once fitted, greasing the pin should not be neglected; a rod end run dry quickly wears oval and develops play. As the play grows, the cylinder knocks on every reversal — that noise is the signal that the rod end is due for replacement. For the cylinder itself see «Hydraulic Cylinders», and for the seal group see «Hydraulic Seals, Nutrings and Wipers».

sss.s: Is a rod end really necessary?
sss.c: It is necessary in any application where there is the slightest axis misalignment between load and cylinder — which in practice means almost all of them. In a rigid connection, misalignment is carried into the rod as side load; the seal leaks on one side and the rod bends over time. Only where the load is guided and the axis is guaranteed, as in bench-type mountings, can a rigid connection be used.

sss.s: Is rod end size chosen from the rod diameter?
sss.c: No. The size of a rod end is the diameter of its pin bore: 20 mm on a PR20, 50 mm on an S 50 N. It is determined by the pin carrying the load. Rod diameter matters only on the threaded type, and only so that the thread at the rod end matches.

sss.s: What is the difference between threaded and weld-on types?
sss.c: The threaded type (PR series) screws onto the thread at the cylinder rod end and can be removed; it is preferred where the rod will be changed during maintenance. The weld-on type (S series) is welded to the machine frame and is generally used at the rear mounting of the cylinder. Most applications use both together: threaded at the rod end, weld-on at the rear.

sss.s: What do C and N mean in the S series?
sss.c: They denote body shape. C is a round body, N a rectangular one. The pin bore does the same job in both; the choice depends on the shape of the surface to be welded and the space available at the mounting. A rectangular body gives a wider weld area on a flat surface.

sss.s: The cylinder knocks on every reversal — what causes it?
sss.c: Usually play in the rod end pin. An ungreased rod end wears oval over time; when the cylinder reverses it travels freely through that clearance and strikes the pin. As the noise grows, so does the play, and the pin begins to wear as well. The remedy is to replace the rod end and grease it regularly.

h1: Ball Valves, Butterfly Valves and Shut-off Components
ozet: Mini ball valves, full-bore ball valves and butterfly valves; for hydraulic and fluid lines.
giris:
A shut-off valve is the component used to open and close a line. This is what distinguishes it from a control valve: a control valve directs and regulates flow, while a shut-off valve is mostly two-position — open or closed.

A ball valve operates by turning a bored ball inside it a quarter turn; when fully open, it offers almost no resistance to flow and allows fast shut-off. This is why it's standard on maintenance and safety lines. A butterfly valve, by contrast, is more economical and lighter in larger diameters, but since the disc remains in the flow path even when fully open, it creates some pressure loss. For valves used on hydraulic lines, it must always be confirmed that the rated pressure exceeds the system pressure.

sss.s: How do I choose between a ball valve and a butterfly valve?
sss.c: For small and medium diameters, where full sealing and low pressure loss are required, a ball valve is the right choice. For large diameters (DN100 and above), a butterfly valve is both lighter and more economical, offering an advantage in space and cost.

sss.s: Can I use the valve in a half-open position?
sss.c: A ball valve is not designed for throttling. In a half-open position, the edge of the ball and the seat surface wear quickly, and the valve will eventually leak. If flow needs to be regulated, a flow control valve should be used instead.

sss.s: Which pressure class should I choose for hydraulic applications?
sss.c: The valve's rated pressure (PN) must exceed the system's peak pressure — looking only at the working pressure is not enough. In hydraulic circuits, pressure spikes can rise well above the working value, so a safety margin should be allowed.

h1: Pressure Gauge Types: Glycerine-Filled, Dry, Diaphragm and Contact Gauges
ozet: Pressure gauges with Ø40, Ø63 and Ø100 mm dials, from 0-1 bar to 0-600 bar; bottom and rear connection, dry and glycerine-filled, plus mbar-range diaphragm types.
giris:
The pressure gauge is the simplest and most frequently consulted instrument in a hydraulic or pneumatic circuit. Almost every fault-finding exercise begins by reading a gauge: is the pump building pressure, is the relief valve opening early, is the line blocked — the answer shows up on the needle.

Five values govern the selection. First, dial size: Ø40 for tight panels and machine mounting, Ø63 for general use, Ø100 where a power unit has to be read from a distance. Second, the measuring range. The rule is that normal working pressure should fall at about two thirds of the scale; a circuit running at 150 bar suits a 0-250 bar gauge. A 0-600 bar gauge will also show 150 bar, but the needle sits at the start of the scale, so resolution is poor and small changes go unnoticed.

Third, connection orientation: bottom connection for piped installations and machine mounting, rear connection for gauges recessed into a panel face. Fourth, filling. A glycerine-filled gauge has a liquid-filled case; that liquid damps the needle so it does not jump with vibration, and it protects the movement from fatigue. On pump outlets, cylinder lines and mobile hydraulics — anywhere with pulsation — a filled gauge is all but mandatory. A dry gauge is adequate on vibration-free fixed lines and costs less.

Fifth, the type. A standard Bourdon-tube gauge measures in bar. At low pressure — ventilation, filter contamination, food and process lines — the millibar range is needed, and a diaphragm gauge is used instead. Vacuum gauges read the negative side. Contact gauges (NCNO) close an electrical contact when a set pressure is reached, so they can stop a pump or raise an alarm; they control as well as indicate.

A gauge is rarely piped directly into the line — it usually goes through a gauge adaptor or reverse fitting, and those parts are listed in this group as well. Where pressure surges are severe, a throttle or a protective isolating valve is fitted upstream; without one, even a robust gauge loses its needle within a few months.

sss.s: What pressure range should I choose?
sss.c: Normal working pressure should fall at roughly two thirds of the scale. For a circuit running at 150 bar, 0-250 bar is the right choice. Too wide a scale costs reading resolution; too narrow a scale lets pressure surges drive the needle against the stop and damage the movement.

sss.s: Why choose a glycerine-filled gauge?
sss.c: The glycerine in the case damps needle flutter caused by pressure pulsation. This both makes the gauge readable and slows wear in the geared movement. Filled gauges are used on pump outlets, cylinder lines and mobile hydraulics. On vibration-free fixed lines a dry gauge is sufficient.

sss.s: Bottom or rear connection?
sss.c: Use bottom connection if the gauge screws straight into pipework or sits on the machine. Use rear connection if it is recessed into a panel face and read from the front. There is no difference in measurement, only in mounting orientation — and this is the single most common cause of ordering the wrong part.

sss.s: When is a diaphragm gauge required?
sss.c: When the pressure to be measured is in millibars rather than bar, a standard Bourdon-tube gauge cannot resolve it. Diaphragm types are used on ventilation ducts, filter contamination measurement, and low-pressure process and food lines. They also prevent the Bourdon tube from clogging with viscous or particle-laden media.

sss.s: What does a contact gauge do?
sss.c: A contact gauge (NCNO) closes an electrical contact when the set pressure is reached. That signal can stop a pump, sound an alarm or drive a valve. In simple systems it removes the need for a separate pressure switch, acting as indicator and threshold switch at once.

sss.s: The needle no longer returns to zero — what happened?
sss.c: If pressure has been released but the needle stays above zero, the Bourdon tube has been permanently stretched, meaning the gauge has been over-pressurised. It will no longer read accurately and must not be used for setting pressures. To prevent a repeat, move to a wider scale or fit a throttle in the line.

h1: O-Ring Sizes, O-Ring Cord and Gaskets
ozet: O-rings in NBR and FKM (Viton) in metric and inch sizes. Cylinder seals, rod seals and wipers are a separate group.
giris:
The O-ring is the most common type of seal, sealing by being compressed between two mating surfaces. Two values determine the correct selection: size (inner diameter × cross-section diameter) and material.

Material selection depends on the fluid and the operating temperature. NBR is the standard choice for general hydraulic oils and operates roughly between -30 °C and +100 °C. FKM (Viton) is used for high temperatures and aggressive fluids. EPDM is suitable for water and brake fluid but must never be used with mineral oil — this is the most common material mistake made in the field.

The O-ring is only one part of a complete sealing set. The nutrings, piston seals, wipers, and wear rings that do the main work in hydraulic cylinders form a separate category and make up a much larger share of our stock (5,297 items); see the «Hydraulic Seals, Nutrings and Wipers» page for those.

sss.s: How do I read an O-ring size?
sss.c: O-ring size is given as inner diameter × cross-section (cord) diameter. For example, 20×2.5 means a 20 mm inner diameter and a 2.5 mm cross-section. Measurement should be taken unstretched, preferably with calipers; a used O-ring may be permanently deformed, which makes its measured size misleading.

sss.s: Should I choose NBR or FKM?
sss.c: For standard mineral-based hydraulic oil at normal operating temperatures, NBR is sufficient and more economical. FKM is preferred in applications where temperature is continuously above 100 °C, or where there is contact with fuel or chemicals.

sss.s: Why is EPDM not used with hydraulic oil?
sss.c: EPDM swells on contact with mineral oil and loses its sealing properties. It is the correct choice for water-based fluids and brake fluid; mineral-oil systems should use NBR or FKM instead.

ad: Hydraulic Seals, Rod Seals and Wipers
h1: Hydraulic Seals, Rod Seals and Wipers — by Kastaş Profile Code
ozet: Rod and piston seals, rod seals, wipers, guide rings and back-up rings. Over 5,290 sizes in stock across K21, K06, K22, K23, K33 and other Kastaş profiles.
giris:
No single part seals a hydraulic cylinder on its own. On the rod side, the rod seal and gland seal; on the piston side, the piston seal; against the outside, the wiper (dust wiper); the load-bearing guide ring; and the back-up ring that supports the seal from behind at high pressure — all work together. During an overhaul the entire set is usually replaced; replacing only the leaking part often brings the same failure back within a short time.

At Kastaş, every profile has a code: K21, K06, K22, K23, K33 and so on. Ordering requires two pieces of information: the profile code and three dimensions. Dimensions are always written as three numbers — for example K21-040/11 (40 × 50 × 8): two diameters and a height.

The order of the dimensions also tells you where the part fits. If the numbers increase (40 × 50), the part goes onto the rod; if they decrease (63 × 51), it fits onto the piston. In our stock this distinction holds consistently by code: K21, K22, K06, K33, K68 and K37 are rod-side; K23, K18, K69 and K17 are piston-side.

The material is written at the end of the code. PU (polyurethane) is the most wear-resistant option and the standard choice in mobile hydraulics; NBR is an economical solution for mineral-oil systems; FKM (Viton) is for high temperatures and aggressive fluids. The same profile is often stocked in both PU and NBR versions — half of the 1,223 sizes in the K21 family are PU.

If you don't know the profile code, that's not a problem: a photo of the removed part along with the rod diameter, bore diameter and height is enough. Take the measurement from a cleaned, unstretched part, preferably with a caliper; a seal that has been under pressure can deform permanently, so a visual estimate can be misleading.

sss.s: What is K21 and where is it used?
sss.c: K21 is Kastaş's rod seal profile code and the largest sealing family in our stock — we carry 1,223 different sizes. Because its dimensions increase from the inner diameter to the outer diameter (e.g. K21-040/11 · 40 × 50 × 8), it fits onto the rod. It is available in PU, NBR and FKM.

sss.s: What information do I need to provide to order a seal?
sss.c: The profile code and three dimensions: inner diameter, outer diameter and height. If you know the code (e.g. K06-040 PU), that alone is enough — we look up the matching dimensions from the code. If you don't have the code, send the three dimensions and a photo of the part.

sss.s: Which should I choose: PU, NBR or FKM?
sss.c: PU (polyurethane) is the most wear-resistant; it is the standard choice for high-pressure applications and mobile machinery. NBR is economical and sufficient for mineral-oil systems at normal temperatures. FKM (Viton) is used where there is continuous high temperature, or contact with fuel or chemicals.

sss.s: I don't know the profile code — how do you find the right seal?
sss.c: Send a clear photo of the removed part along with its three dimensions. The profile's cross-section (rod seal, U-profile, wiper, guide ring) can be identified from the photo, and the dimensions point us to the matching item in stock. When measuring a used part, keep in mind it may be deformed — if possible, also measure the cylinder's rod and bore diameter.

sss.s: Can I just replace the leaking seal on its own?
sss.c: You can, but it often doesn't last long. The leak is usually caused by a worn guide ring letting the rod run off-center, or a wiper letting dust through; in that case the new seal wears out just as fast. Since the cylinder is already disassembled, replacing the entire set is also cheaper in terms of labor.

h1: Hydraulic Repair Kits: JCB Cylinder and Hema Pump Seal Sets
ozet: Complete seal sets for a given cylinder or pump in a single package: Kastaş JB-991 series JCB kits, Hema 1PN/1P1/2P1 pump kits and hydraulic motor repair kits.
giris:
Open up a leaking cylinder or pump and you are left holding a handful of sealing elements: piston seal, rod seal, wiper, guide rings, O-rings and back-up rings. Measuring and sourcing each of them one by one takes time and carries risk — if a single item is missing or comes in the wrong size, the machine has to come apart again.

A repair kit removes that problem: every sealing element for a given cylinder or pump model arrives in one package, in the correct size and the correct material. The most expensive part of an overhaul is not the parts but the time the machine stands idle; using a kit shortens it.

Stock covers three families. The first is the Kastaş JB-991 series for construction machinery cylinders; the codes carry the original JCB number (JB-991/00110, for example) and are searched by that number directly. The second is the Hema 0P1, 1P1, 1PN, 2P1 and 3P1 series kits for pumps, matched by the series code on the pump label. The third is the MR, MH, MM and MT series kits for hydraulic motors. Seal kits for pneumatic cylinders are also carried.

The one critical piece of information when ordering a kit is the model and serial number. Two cylinders that look the same bore may use different seal profiles; it is model matching, not dimension matching, that counts. Where the label cannot be read, you have to work from the size and profile of the seals removed — in that case selecting items individually is safer than a kit; for profile codes see the «Hydraulic Seals, Nutrings and Wipers» page.

Two points must not be skipped during assembly. Seals should be lubricated with system oil before fitting, and an assembly sleeve used where they pass over sharp corners and threads — most early leaks come from a seal cut during installation. Second, the condition of the rod and bore surfaces should be checked while the seals are renewed; a new seal fitted to a scored rod will leak again before long.

sss.s: Should I buy a repair kit or select the seals individually?
sss.c: If the model of the cylinder or pump is known, a kit is always safer: every element arrives complete, in the correct profile and size. If the model is unknown, or the machine has previously been repaired with non-original parts, the kit may not fit; in that case measure the elements removed and select item by item.

sss.s: How do I order a JCB repair kit?
sss.c: Search by the original JCB number; the items carry that number (JB-991/00110, for example). It is read from the label on the cylinder or from the machine's spare parts catalogue. If the number cannot be read, supply the cylinder's rod diameter, bore and stroke together with the machine model and year.

sss.s: What does a kit contain?
sss.c: A cylinder kit typically contains the piston seal, rod seal, wiper, guide (wear) rings, O-rings and back-up rings. Pump kits contain the shaft seal, housing O-rings and, where applicable, wear plate gaskets. Springs, bearings and metal parts are not included and are ordered separately.

sss.s: I fitted a new kit and it still leaks — why?
sss.c: There are two common causes. The first is assembly damage: the seal was cut as it passed over a thread or a sharp corner. Seals should be lubricated and fitted using an assembly sleeve. The second is surface condition: if the rod is scored lengthwise, or the chrome plating is flaking, no seal will hold and the rod must be renewed.

sss.s: Can the seal material in a kit be changed?
sss.c: Standard kits are produced for mineral-based hydraulic oil at normal temperatures. If the system runs continuously hot, or uses a water-based fluid, the material has to be selected accordingly. In that case it is right to select the elements individually in a suitable material rather than take a ready-made kit.
